title: D) Design for performance
text:
Normally in feedback \(e=r-y\) rewriting this gives: \[\begin{equation}
\frac{e}{r} = \frac{1}{1+HC} = S
\end{equation}\]
when using this y can be written as: \[\begin{equation}
y = \frac{H}{1+HC}d=S\cdot Hd
\end{equation}\]
So therefore feedback is: - advantageous when \(|S|<1\) - disadvantageous when \(|S| > 1\)
However due to the bode sensitivity integral you cannot just ensure that \(|S|\) is always lower than 1. Becuase the area beneath \(|S|\) is always non-negative. Therefore shaping \(|S|\) is like a waterbed suppression for 1 frequency leads to a amplification elsewhere. This holds only where the open loops \(L(s)\) with relative degree 2 or higher.

title: F) Sampled systems and discrete-time domain
text:
Discrete time systems
Differentiation in time domain is actually the same as difference in discrete time domain because you are just measuring the difference in time stamp k and time stamp k+1. That is why you can write this also down as: \[
\begin{aligned}
x(k+1)&=zx(k)\\
x(k-1)&=z^{-1}x(k)\\
x(k-N)&=z^{-N}x(k)
\end{aligned}
\] This means that the shift operator z is the discrete counterpart of laplace variable s: \[\begin{equation}
\dot{x}(s) = sx(s) <-> x(k+1) = zx(k)
\end{equation}\]

title: F) Sampled systems and discrete-time domain
section: How to convert controller from continuous to discretized time?
text:
How to convert controller from continuous to discretized time?



image.png



Time domain approximations
In this we have to make assumptions on behaviour of \(u(t)\) between samples. Aka we have to assume waht the controller is doing between t(k) and t(k+1). for eurler this is to hold so \(u(t)\) is constant between samples for Tusin, this means that there is a linear change from u(k-1) to u(k). For the upcoming explanation we are going to use continuous time integrator \(C(s) = \frac{1}{s}\). To explain how to achieve this. Btw a integrator is basically trying to calculate the surface beneath the curve \(u(t)\).
For euler there are two methods one is called the forward euler. This is based on the forward difference quotient: \[
\begin{aligned}
\dot{y}(t)&=u(t)\\
\dot{y}(t)&\approx \frac{y(t+T)-y(t)}{T} =>\frac{y(k+1)-y(k)}{T} = u(k)
\end{aligned}
\]
Shifting this in time gives: \[
\frac{y(k)-y(k-1)}{T} = u(k)
\] Which can be rewritten to: \[
y(k) = y(k-1) + Tu(k-1)
\]
this gives the approximation: \[
C(z)=\frac{Tz^{-1}}{1-z^{-1}}=\frac{T}{z-1}
\]



image.png


Backward euler works like this:



image.png


It uses the current sample to estimate the area where forward uses the previous sample.
Tustin does the same however that takes the average value of the current input and the previous input. 
Tustin works best of these methods however they do not give a guarantee that it working well. See for example the image below. 


Tustin with prewarping
tustin with prewarping is that you match the frequency responses of \(C(z)\) and \(C(s)\) at a specified freq \(\omega_p\). 


Pole-zero matching
In here you try to map all poles and zeros to the discrete domain.  Although phase is different in discrete domain so it will never be exactly the same. 
In practice tustin with prewarping is the best!

The power per frequency is called the power spectral density (PSD). Using therefore RMS and parseval theorem and given the complex fourier series that results in:

To find whether 2 signals are simalar you compute CPSD of several frames of the signals and average them. Therefore averaging has affect on the outcome of this.  You multiply with the complex conjugate of the input Fourier transform. Such that it sets up the math to isolate correlated signals from uncorrelated noise using CPSD. title: E) Feedforward
text:
Trajectory planning is a technique in which you simplify the trajectory which ensures that the error gets lower. Most often uses more differentiable signals. This leads to: - less oscillations - possibly faster settling times - smaller control signals
The DC-gain is the steady-state ain of a system where \(\omega\) is 0. Often this is $
Feedforward is added to after the controller. Mostly the feedforward should actually be the inverse of the plant. However if the plant is unstable or unknown then we need to approximate the inverse of the plant in the time domain. Generally you forward the forces that are needed to: - accelerate the rigid body mode of the plant \(F_a = K_{fa}\ddot x_s\) - overcome the viscous friction with the fixed world: \(F_v = K_{fv} \dot x_s\) - overcome the coulomb friction with the fixed world: \(F_c = K_{fc} \cdot sign(\dot x_s)\)

title: E) Feedforward
text:
Tuning of Feedforward



image.png


The best trajectory to tune the parameters is approx 1/3 acceleration, 1/3 constant velocity, 1/3 deceleration.
First the \(K_{fc}\) should be tuned. In such a way that the deceleration of the forward movement and acceleration of the backward movement have the same error.
Secondly the \(K_{fv}\) must be tunes. There should be no error during constant velocity phases when \(K_{fc}\) and \(K_{fv}\) are correct.
Thirdly \(K_{fa}\) must be tuned to minize the error during acceleration and deceleration.
For this tuning the feedback controller should be just good enough to reasonably control the plant but should be not too good such that the error deminishes. The frequency of the reference signal should be such that the magnitude of the closed loop sensitivity is around -40. Or the bandwidth $f_{bw} hz $ where \(t_{phase}\) is the length of each phase.

title: C) Stability
text:
When using a feedback controller the poles become the zeros. However everytime checking how these poles changes based on the controller is not really feasible or intuitive, that is why nyquist criterion is designed
This criterion is based on encirclements the number of clockwise encirclements of the origin is denoted by \(N=Z-P\) in which Z is the number of enclosed zeors and P is the number of enclosed poles. this is evaluated on 1 + L(s) because: - Poles of 1 + L(s) -> open-loop poles - Zeros of 1 + L(s) -> closed-loop poles
The closed loop is stable when \(Z\) is 0 and therefore \(Z=N+P=0\)
However this can be simplified to instead of 1+L(s) encirclements of origin to just L(s) encirclements of point(-1,0)
This can be translated to the bode plot and therefore a bode plot (L(s)) has the following necessary conditions for stability: - Slope $ at \(w_{co}\) - the phase must be between -180 and 0, therefore the curve meest keep (-1,0) to its left. - It must enter the unit disc to its left
However the following sufficient conditions must also hold: - All poles and zeros of \(L(S)=C(s)H(s)\) must lie strictly in the LHP - Single crossover. The magnitude crosses 0dB once and never crosses it again.

title: C) Stability
text:
Stability Margins
A system is stable or not however it does have some robustness measurements. These are also called phase margin and gain margin. They are also provided in the plot below.
The PM is the phase lead above -180 at the frequency where \(|L(s)| = 0dB\),
The inverse of GM is the gain at the frequency where \(\angle L(j\omega) = -180^\circ\)
The modulus margin (MM) is the inverse of the smallest distance of \(L(j\omega)\) over all \(\omega\) to the point -1. The distance of the point -1 to \(L(j\omega)\) is given by: \[L(j\omega) - (-1) = 1 + L(j\omega)\]
Note that the modulus margin is therefore the minimal value of this function. Also know that the Sensitivity is given as: \[S(j\omega) = \frac{1}{1 + L(j\omega)}\] Therefore sensitivity is the inverse of the distance and therefore the minimal value of the distance function is the same as the maximal value of the sensitivity function.
